title: Review: Metallic bonding and comparing structures; Giant covalent structures; Periodic table structure and blocks; Periodic trends
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for Eduqas A-level Chemistry (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: PT01#t1 term and clue written for the game; BD06#t2 term and clue written for the game; BD05#t2 term and clue written for the game; BD05#t1 term and clue written for the game. Questions: BD05#N.11a, BD06#N.15, PT01#N.6, PT02#N.6, BD05#N.10, BD06#N.3a, PT01#N.12a, PT02#N.10, BD05#N.7, BD06#N.11, PT02#N.12, PT02#N.14. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Period
items.clue: A row of the table; its number gives the outer occupied shell.

items.label: Alloy
items.clue: A mixture such as brass or steel, usually harder and stronger than the pure metal.

items.label: Graphite
items.clue: Flat layers of hexagons that slide over each other, so it is soft, yet it conducts.

items.label: Diamond
items.clue: Each C is joined to four others, tetrahedrally, in 3D; very hard and does not conduct.

questions.stem: Graphite conducts electricity far better along its layers than at right angles to them. Which statement explains this?

options.text: Its layers slide over each other, and charge is carried only in the direction they slide.
Its ions lie between the layers, so they can move only in the plane of the layers.
Each atom forms four bonds within its layer, so no electrons are left to pass between layers.
Its delocalised electrons move freely within a layer, but cannot easily cross the gap to the next.

questions.explanation: Each C bonds to three others; its fourth electron is delocalised over its own layer only. So charge flows easily along a layer, but hardly between layers.

questions.stem: Each liquid is tested with two electrodes and a bulb. Which liquid will not conduct electricity?

options.text: Molten sodium chloride at 850 °C
Liquid mercury at 20 °C
Liquid titanium(IV) chloride, TiCl₄, at 20 °C
Molten aluminium at 700 °C

questions.explanation: TiCl₄ (boils at 136 °C) is made of small covalent molecules. With no ions and no delocalised electrons, nothing carries charge, even though titanium is a metal.

questions.stem: Germanium is in period 4, group 14. Which is the full electron configuration of a germanium atom?

options.text: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s² 4p²
1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d² 4s²
1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d¹⁰ 4s² 4p²
1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d¹⁰ 4s² 4p⁴

questions.explanation: Period 4, p-block: fill up to 4p. Group 14 gives 14 − 10 = 4 valence electrons, 4s² 4p². With the 3d¹⁰, the total is 32 electrons.

questions.stem: The first ionisation energy of magnesium is lower than that of beryllium. Which explains this?

options.text: Magnesium has more electrons, so the nucleus's pull is shared among more of them.
Magnesium's outer electron is in shell 3, further from the nucleus and more shielded.
Magnesium's 3s electrons are paired, and their repulsion makes one easy to remove.
Magnesium is more reactive, so it gives up its outer electron more readily.

questions.explanation: Mg is [Ne] 3s², Be is 1s² 2s². The extra shell adds distance and shielding, which outweigh the larger nuclear charge (+12 against +4), so less energy is needed.

questions.stem: Hexagonal boron nitride has a layered structure like graphite, but it does not conduct electricity. Which statement explains this?

options.text: Its spare electrons are held on the more electronegative N atoms, so they cannot move along the layers.
Its layers are much further apart than in graphite, so electrons cannot pass from one to the next.
It is made of B³⁺ and N³⁻ ions, which are held in fixed positions in the solid.
Each atom forms four covalent bonds, so no electrons are left over to carry a current.

questions.explanation: In graphite the fourth electron of each C is delocalised across the layer. In hexagonal BN the electron density stays on N, so no charge carriers move.

questions.stem: Aluminium is rolled into kitchen foil less than 0.02 mm thick without cracking. Which statement explains this property of aluminium?

options.text: Its layers of cations slide, staying attracted to the delocalised electrons around them.
Its metallic bonds are weak, so the rollers can easily push its atoms apart.
Its bonds between neighbouring atoms bend like hinges instead of breaking.
Its individual atoms are soft, so each one is flattened as it passes between the rollers.

questions.explanation: Metallic bonding is non-directional, so the delocalised electrons keep attracting the cations after the layers have slid. The metal changes shape without cracking.

questions.stem: Beryllium, 1s² 2s², and helium, 1s², both have two electrons in their outer s sub-shell. Why is beryllium placed in group 2, but helium in group 18?

options.text: Beryllium is a solid and helium is a gas, and group 18 holds the gaseous elements.
Beryllium has four electrons and helium two, and the group number counts the total.
Beryllium's 2s² electrons are in a higher shell, so they are inner electrons, not valence electrons.
Beryllium's outer shell, n = 2, is far from full, while helium's n = 1 shell is full with just two.

questions.stem: Fluorine is more electronegative than chlorine. Which explains this?

options.text: A fluorine atom has more protons than a chlorine atom, so it pulls harder on a shared pair.
Fluorine needs only one electron to fill its outer shell, so it attracts electrons strongly.
In fluorine the shared pair is closer to the nucleus and shielded by fewer inner electrons.
Fluorine releases more energy than chlorine when it gains an electron, so it is more electronegative.

questions.explanation: Fluorine's bonding electrons are in shell 2, shielded only by 1s². Chlorine's are in shell 3, shielded by 10 inner electrons. Shorter distance and less shielding outweigh chlorine's larger nuclear charge.

questions.stem: Substance X melts at 1710 °C. It does not conduct electricity, either as a solid or when molten. It does not dissolve in water or in hexane. Which structure does X have?

options.text: A lattice of oppositely charged ions
A network of atoms joined by covalent bonds throughout
A lattice of metal cations in a sea of delocalised electrons
Separate small molecules with very strong forces between them

questions.explanation: The very high melting point means strong bonds break. No conduction even when molten means no ions and no delocalised electrons. Insoluble everywhere: a covalent network.

questions.stem: Four solids, P, Q, R and S, are tested. - P: melts at 801 °C; conducts when molten but not as a solid; dissolves in water. - Q: melts at 1085 °C; conducts as a solid and when molten; insoluble in water. - R: melts at 114 °C; does not conduct as a solid or when molten; insoluble in water. - S: melts at 1710 °C; does not conduct as a solid or when molten; insoluble in water. Which pairing of substance and structure is correct?

options.text: P is metallic, because it conducts when molten.
Q is ionic, because it conducts when molten.
R is molecular, because it melts low and never conducts.
S is ionic, because its melting point is very high.

questions.stem: Why does silicon have the highest melting point of the Period 3 elements?

options.text: It is a giant covalent lattice, so melting breaks many strong covalent bonds.
Its Si₂ molecules have the strongest London forces in the period.
It has four delocalised electrons per atom, so its metallic bonding is the strongest.
Its atoms have the most electrons in the period, so the forces between them are the strongest.

questions.explanation: Each Si atom is covalently bonded to four others in a giant lattice. All those strong bonds must be broken, which needs far more energy than overcoming London forces or the metallic bonding in Al.

questions.stem: An argon atom has seven more electrons than a sodium atom, yet argon's first ionisation energy is about three times sodium's. Which explains this?

options.text: Argon's outer shell is full, and a full shell is stable, so it does not want to lose an electron.
Argon has more electrons, so the extra electron–electron repulsion holds its outer electron in place.
Argon's outer electron is in a higher shell than sodium's, so it is held more tightly.
Argon has 18 protons to sodium's 11, and its outer electrons are in the same shell with similar shielding.
